title: Neoplasms of the Nervous System
subject: Nervous System (NEUR)
author: Dr. Sharilyn Rennie

overview.intro: This chapter covers the primary tumors of the brain, meninges, and peripheral nerves, the neural crest tumor neuroblastoma, brain metastases and primary CNS lymphoma, the two classic eye tumors, and the inherited syndromes that predispose to nervous system tumors. Board questions usually give three clues: the patient's age, the tumor's location, and one histologic or molecular feature. This chapter explains why each clue appears: why childhood tumors favor the posterior fossa, why glioblastoma necroses and enhances in a ring, why a germline tumor suppressor mutation produces bilateral or multiple tumors, and why the location of a mass, more than its grade, decides the symptoms.
prerequisites: Cell types of nervous tissue: neurons, astrocytes, oligodendrocytes, ependymal cells, Schwann cells, and meningothelial cells
CSF production and flow through the ventricles, foramina, and subarachnoid space
Neural crest derivatives: sympathetic ganglia, adrenal medulla, Schwann cells, and melanocytes
Oncogenes, tumor suppressor genes, and the Knudson two-hit hypothesis
Catecholamine synthesis and breakdown by MAO and COMT

connections.how: Ras, RB, HIF, and mTOR pathways explain how single gene losses in NF1, retinoblastoma, VHL, and tuberous sclerosis produce tumors.
NF1, NF2, tuberous sclerosis, VHL, and hereditary retinoblastoma are autosomal dominant at the family level but need a second hit in each tumor cell.
Many tumors cause symptoms by blocking CSF pathways or adding volume to a closed skull rather than by destroying tissue.
Primary CNS lymphoma and toxoplasmosis both appear as ring-enhancing lesions when CD4 counts are very low.
Clear cell renal carcinoma and pheochromocytoma link VHL and NF1 to the kidney and adrenal medulla.

terms.def: Located outside the brain parenchyma, as with a dura-based meningioma, so the tumor compresses rather than infiltrates the brain.
A glioma whose cells migrate individually into surrounding brain, so it has no true margin and cannot be removed completely.
A tumor of primitive cells with dark nuclei and scant cytoplasm on H and E stain, such as medulloblastoma, neuroblastoma, and retinoblastoma.
A ring of tumor nuclei around a central tangle of fibrillary cell processes without a lumen, a sign of neuronal differentiation.
A zone of necrosis bordered by tumor cells lined up at its edge, the defining necrosis pattern of glioblastoma.
A laminated, concentric calcification formed by dystrophic calcification within a tumor, typical of meningioma.
A brightly eosinophilic, corkscrew-shaped aggregate of GFAP and other proteins in astrocytic processes, typical of pilocytic astrocytoma.
Two rows of palisaded Schwann cell nuclei separated by a fibrillary zone, found in the Antoni A areas of schwannoma.
Seeding of tumor cells through the CSF onto the spinal cord, nerve roots, or cauda equina.
A mutation in isocitrate dehydrogenase that makes the enzyme produce 2-hydroxyglutarate and defines the astrocytoma and oligodendroglioma lineage.
Displacement and compression of brain by a tumor and its edema within the fixed volume of the skull.
A disorganized overgrowth of cell types native to a site, as in the cortical tubers of tuberous sclerosis.

blocks.text: Medulloblastoma is the most common malignant brain tumor of childhood, and most patients are diagnosed before age 10. It is an embryonal tumor, meaning it is made of primitive precursor cells that have not differentiated, and it is classified as CNS WHO grade 4. The classic site of medulloblastoma is the cerebellar vermis, in the roof of the fourth ventricle; tumors in older children and adults more often arise laterally in a cerebellar hemisphere.

Under the microscope the tumor forms dense sheets of small cells with dark, crowded nuclei and very little cytoplasm, the pattern called a small round blue cell tumor. Some cells arrange themselves in Homer Wright rosettes, rings of nuclei around a central tangle of neuritic processes with no lumen. These rosettes and staining for synaptophysin show that the tumor is attempting neuronal differentiation. Medulloblastoma is now also divided into molecular groups: WNT-activated tumors have the best prognosis, SHH-activated tumors arise from cerebellar granule cell precursors and occur in Gorlin syndrome (germline PTCH1) and Li-Fraumeni syndrome (germline TP53), and group 3 tumors, often MYC amplified, do worst.
Why the symptoms appear

A vermian mass presses directly on the fourth ventricle, the outflow path for CSF from the lateral and third ventricles. Blocking it produces obstructive (noncommunicating) hydrocephalus. Headache and vomiting are typically worst on waking because intracranial pressure rises when the child lies flat and when nocturnal hypoventilation raises arterial CO2, which dilates cerebral vessels. Raised pressure also causes papilledema and sometimes a sixth nerve palsy, a false localizing sign from stretching of the long intracranial course of the abducens nerve. In infants with open sutures, the head enlarges instead. Damage to the vermis itself causes truncal ataxia with a wide-based, unsteady gait, while limb coordination may be relatively spared.

Because the tumor sits against the CSF pathway, cells shed into the CSF and settle by gravity on the spinal cord, nerve roots, and cauda equina as drop metastases. For this reason staging examines the entire neuraxis and the CSF, not only the posterior fossa.

steps: Embryonal tumor grows in the cerebellar vermis
Morning headache, vomiting, papilledema, sixth nerve palsy
blocks.caption: Obstructive hydrocephalus explains the early pressure symptoms; vermis damage separately explains truncal ataxia.

blocks.title: Common posterior fossa tumors of childhood
rows: Small round blue cells, Homer Wright rosettes

blocks.caption: Children have mostly infratentorial tumors and adults mostly supratentorial ones; location and histology together identify the tumor.

blocks.text: Meningioma is the most common primary intracranial tumor in adults. It arises from arachnoid cap (meningothelial) cells, which cluster in the arachnoid villi and granulations along the dural venous sinuses. The tumor is attached to the dura and lies outside the brain parenchyma, so it is extra-axial: it pushes the brain aside rather than growing into it. It is most common in middle-aged and older adults, and intracranial meningiomas are about twice as common in women as in men. Many tumors express progesterone receptors, which fits the female predominance and the occasional growth during pregnancy.

The two best established risk factors both damage growth control in meningothelial cells. Loss of the NF2 gene on chromosome 22, which encodes the tumor suppressor merlin, is found in about half of sporadic meningiomas, and patients with NF2 often have multiple meningiomas. Ionizing radiation to the head, for example childhood cranial irradiation, increases risk after a latency of many years, and radiation-induced tumors are more often multiple and higher grade.

The classic histology is whorls of meningothelial cells, some of which calcify in concentric layers to form psammoma bodies. The cells stain for epithelial membrane antigen. Most meningiomas are CNS WHO grade 1. Brain invasion or high mitotic activity defines atypical (grade 2) tumors, and frankly malignant histology defines anaplastic (grade 3) tumors. On imaging the tumor is a well-circumscribed, uniformly enhancing dural mass, often with a tapering dural tail and thickening (hyperostosis) of the overlying bone.

Symptoms come from compression and depend on location. Irritation of the underlying cortex causes focal seizures, and pressure on cortex or cranial nerves causes focal deficits. Because growth is slow, the brain adapts, so meningiomas can become large before causing symptoms and many are found incidentally.

blocks.title: Meningioma location predicts the deficit
rows: Parasagittal or falx (near the paracentral lobule)
Leg area of motor and sensory cortex
Contralateral leg weakness or numbness; both legs if bilateral
Focal seizures, focal weakness, or language deficit
Anosmia, personality change; later optic nerve compression
Optic nerve, CN III, IV, VI
Hearing loss and facial numbness, mimicking schwannoma
blocks.caption: Meningioma causes symptoms by mass effect, so the site of the dural attachment predicts the deficit.

blocks.text: Neural crest cells migrate from the dorsal neural tube to form the sympathetic chain ganglia and the chromaffin cells of the adrenal medulla. Neuroblastoma is a malignant tumor of these sympathetic precursor cells. It is the most common extracranial solid tumor of childhood and the most common cancer of infancy; the median age at diagnosis is about 18 months, and about 90% of cases are found before age 5. The adrenal medulla is the most common primary site, but the tumor can arise anywhere along the sympathetic chain, including the paraspinal abdomen, posterior mediastinum, neck, and pelvis.

Histologically it is another small round blue cell tumor, with Homer Wright rosettes and a fibrillary background of neuronal processes (neuropil). The cells stain for neuronal markers such as synaptophysin and chromogranin. Maturation toward ganglion cells and Schwannian stroma (ganglioneuroblastoma, ganglioneuroma) improves behavior.

Because the cells are sympathetic precursors, most tumors synthesize catecholamines. Much of the catecholamine is metabolized inside the tumor, so the urine contains high homovanillic acid (HVA) and vanillylmandelic acid (VMA) in about 90% of patients, while sustained hypertension is less prominent than in pheochromocytoma.

blocks.title: Why urinary HVA and VMA rise
steps: Tyrosine converted to L-dopa by tyrosine hydroxylase
Dopamine broken down by MAO and COMT to HVA
Dopamine converted to norepinephrine (some to epinephrine)
Norepinephrine and epinephrine broken down to VMA
blocks.caption: HVA reflects dopamine and VMA reflects norepinephrine and epinephrine, so both rise when sympathetic precursor cells proliferate.

blocks.text: The usual presentation is a firm, irregular abdominal mass in a young child. A retroperitoneal neuroblastoma grows around the aorta and its branches and often crosses the midline. Metastases explain many presentations: bone and marrow (bone pain, limp, cytopenias), liver (hepatomegaly in infants), skin (bluish nodules in infants), and the orbits (proptosis and periorbital bruising). A paraspinal tumor can grow through a neural foramen and compress the spinal cord, and a cervical or upper thoracic tumor can interrupt the sympathetic chain and cause Horner syndrome.

Opsoclonus-myoclonus (rapid chaotic eye movements, limb jerks, and ataxia) is a paraneoplastic syndrome in a small percentage of children, thought to result from antitumor immunity that cross-reacts with neurons. Amplification of the MYCN oncogene, found in about a fifth of tumors, drives proliferation and predicts aggressive disease regardless of age. At the other extreme, some infants with metastatic disease limited to skin, liver, and marrow have tumors that regress spontaneously.

blocks.title: Neuroblastoma compared with Wilms tumor
rows: Irregular, often crosses midline, encases vessels
Smooth, within the kidney, rarely crosses midline
WT1 mutation or 11p15 (WT2) alterations in some cases
blocks.caption: Both present as abdominal masses in young children; origin outside the kidney explains the neuroblastoma features.

blocks.text: Glioblastoma is the most common primary malignant brain tumor in adults, usually in people older than 50. Under the current WHO classification it is defined as a diffuse astrocytic glioma of adults that is IDH-wildtype, and it is always CNS WHO grade 4. Its astrocytic nature is shown by staining for glial fibrillary acidic protein (GFAP), the intermediate filament of astrocytes. IDH-mutant grade 4 astrocytomas, once called secondary glioblastoma, are now classified separately because they arise in younger patients and have a better prognosis.

The tumor arises in the cerebral hemispheres, centered in white matter. Its cells migrate individually along myelinated tracts, so a glioblastoma can cross the corpus callosum to the opposite hemisphere and form a butterfly-shaped mass. Tumor cells are present well beyond the enhancing edge seen on imaging, which is why the tumor recurs even after extensive resection.
Necrosis, new vessels, and the ring

Glioblastoma outgrows its blood supply. The hypoxic center dies, and tumor cells line up along the edge of each necrotic zone (pseudopalisading necrosis), probably as they migrate away from the hypoxic core. Hypoxia stabilizes the transcription factor HIF-1 alpha, which induces vascular endothelial growth factor (VEGF). VEGF drives microvascular proliferation, tufts of multilayered endothelial cells that can look like renal glomeruli. These new vessels lack a normal blood-brain barrier. On contrast imaging this produces a thick, irregular rim of enhancement around a dark necrotic center, surrounded by vasogenic edema from leaky vessels.

blocks.title: Glioblastoma: from hypoxia to ring enhancement
blocks.caption: The same hypoxia-VEGF chain explains the two defining histologic features and the imaging appearance.

blocks.text: Common molecular changes include EGFR amplification, PTEN loss (unchecked PI3K-AKT signaling), CDKN2A deletion (loss of the p16 brake on the RB pathway), and TERT promoter mutation (sustained telomerase). In an IDH-wildtype diffuse astrocytic tumor, TERT promoter mutation, EGFR amplification, or gain of chromosome 7 with loss of chromosome 10 is enough for the diagnosis even before necrosis or microvascular proliferation appears. Methylation of the MGMT promoter silences a DNA repair enzyme that removes alkyl groups from the O6 position of guanine; such tumors repair alkylating DNA damage poorly and have longer survival.
Patients develop headache, seizures, personality change, or focal deficits over weeks to months as the mass and edema expand. Median survival is only about 15 months even with maximal therapy.

sections.title: Pilocytic astrocytoma versus IDH-mutant diffuse gliomas

blocks.text: Gliomas divide into two behaviors. Circumscribed gliomas such as pilocytic astrocytoma form a mass with a border and can often be cured by removal. Diffuse gliomas send single cells into the surrounding brain, so even a slow-growing, low-grade diffuse glioma cannot be completely removed and tends to recur and progress. This growth pattern, more than grade at diagnosis, explains the difference in outcome.

Pilocytic astrocytoma is CNS WHO grade 1 and is the most common brain tumor of children overall. The classic picture is a cerebellar cyst with an enhancing mural nodule; other sites are the optic nerve and chiasm (especially in NF1), hypothalamus, and brainstem. Histology is biphasic: compact areas of elongated, hair-like (piloid) cells containing Rosenthal fibers, and loose microcystic areas with eosinophilic granular bodies. Rosenthal fibers are not specific, since they also appear in chronic reactive gliosis and Alexander disease. Almost all pilocytic astrocytomas carry an alteration that activates the MAPK pathway, most often a KIAA1549-BRAF fusion in cerebellar tumors, less often BRAF V600E or loss of NF1. Prognosis is excellent.

IDH-mutant diffuse gliomas arise mainly in the cerebral hemispheres of young and middle-aged adults, most often the frontal lobe, and frequently present with seizures because they infiltrate cortex. Mutant isocitrate dehydrogenase (most often IDH1 R132H) converts alpha-ketoglutarate to 2-hydroxyglutarate. This oncometabolite inhibits alpha-ketoglutarate dependent enzymes, including TET DNA demethylases and histone demethylases, so DNA becomes widely hypermethylated and cells are held in an undifferentiated, proliferative state.

Two tumors share this IDH-mutant origin. Astrocytoma, IDH-mutant, usually has loss of ATRX and mutation of TP53 and is graded 2 to 4. Oligodendroglioma is defined by IDH mutation plus codeletion of whole chromosome arms 1p and 19q, is graded 2 or 3, and often calcifies. Its cells have round nuclei and clear cytoplasm, the fried-egg appearance (an artifact of delayed fixation), separated by a delicate branching chicken-wire capillary network.

blocks.title: Distinguishing the three gliomas
rows: Frontal lobe, cortex and white matter
blocks.caption: Growth pattern and molecular markers separate these tumors more reliably than appearance alone.

blocks.predict: A 9-year-old has a grade 1 cerebellar tumor and a 35-year-old has a grade 2 frontal tumor. Which patient is more likely to have recurrence after surgery?
blocks.explain: The adult, because an IDH-mutant diffuse glioma infiltrates beyond any visible margin and tends to progress, while a circumscribed pilocytic astrocytoma can be removed whole.
blocks.check: Reread the first paragraph on circumscribed versus diffuse growth.

blocks.text: Most brain tumors arise from glia, because mature neurons do not divide. A small group of tumors, however, contains neoplastic cells with neuronal differentiation, either alone or mixed with neoplastic glia. These tumors are usually low grade, and their symptoms depend on where they sit: in the cortex they cause epilepsy, and in a ventricle they block CSF.

Ganglioglioma is the classic example. It is a slow-growing CNS WHO grade 1 tumor of children and young adults, most often in the temporal lobe. It contains two neoplastic populations: large, abnormal (dysmorphic) ganglion cells, sometimes with two nuclei, and a glial component that is usually astrocytic. Eosinophilic granular bodies, cuffs of lymphocytes around vessels, and calcification are common, and many tumors carry BRAF V600E. On imaging it is often a cortical cyst with an enhancing nodule and little surrounding edema.

The usual presentation is a long history of focal seizures that resist anticonvulsant drugs. The temporal lobe, particularly its mesial structures, has a low seizure threshold, and the abnormal neurons within and around the tumor form excitable networks. Because the tumor grows slowly, raised intracranial pressure is unusual. Dysembryoplastic neuroepithelial tumor (DNT) is another low-grade cortical tumor that presents the same way.

Central neurocytoma is a CNS WHO grade 2 tumor of young adults that grows inside a lateral ventricle, often attached to the septum pellucidum near the foramen of Monro. Its uniform round cells with clear perinuclear halos resemble oligodendroglioma, but they stain for synaptophysin, showing neuronal differentiation, and the tumor arises within the ventricle rather than infiltrating brain. Symptoms come from obstruction of one or both foramina of Monro: the lateral ventricles enlarge and patients develop headache, vomiting, and papilledema. Prognosis is generally favorable.

Dysmorphic ganglion cells plus neoplastic glia; often BRAF V600E
Children and young adults; temporal cortex
Multinodular cortical tumor with neurons floating in mucoid matrix

blocks.text: Schwann cells, derived from the neural crest, myelinate peripheral axons, including cranial nerve axons beyond the short segment myelinated by oligodendrocytes. A schwannoma is a benign, encapsulated CNS WHO grade 1 tumor of Schwann cells. It grows eccentrically from one side of the nerve and pushes the axons aside, so the parent nerve can often be separated from it. Most sporadic schwannomas, like those in NF2, have lost function of the NF2 gene product merlin.

The histology has two patterns. Antoni A areas are densely cellular, with spindle cells whose nuclei line up in palisades; two rows of palisaded nuclei separated by a pink fibrillary zone form a Verocay body. Antoni B areas are loose, hypocellular, and myxoid. The cells stain strongly and uniformly for S-100, a marker of neural crest derived cells.
Vestibular schwannoma at the cerebellopontine angle

The most common intracranial schwannoma arises from the vestibular division of CN VIII inside the internal acoustic canal; the old name acoustic neuroma is inaccurate on both counts. It grows out of the canal into the cerebellopontine angle, the space between the cerebellum, pons, and petrous bone. Compression of the cochlear nerve and its blood supply in the canal causes slowly progressive unilateral sensorineural hearing loss, the most common presenting complaint, often with tinnitus and speech discrimination worse than the pure-tone loss suggests. Vestibular input is lost so slowly that the brain compensates, so patients report imbalance more than true vertigo.

A larger tumor stretches CN V, causing facial numbness and a reduced corneal reflex through loss of its afferent limb. CN VII travels with CN VIII but its motor fibers tolerate stretch, so facial weakness is usually late. Further growth compresses the cerebellar peduncles and hemisphere (ipsilateral limb ataxia) and the fourth ventricle (hydrocephalus).

Bilateral vestibular schwannomas are the hallmark of NF2, an autosomal dominant disorder caused by mutation of NF2 on chromosome 22. Merlin mediates contact inhibition of growth, so a Schwann cell that loses its second copy proliferates. NF2 patients also develop meningiomas, spinal ependymomas, and early posterior subcapsular cataracts.

blocks.title: Localizing a cerebellopontine angle mass
blocks.text: A 48-year-old has a year of worsening left-sided hearing loss and ringing. The Weber test lateralizes to the right ear, and air conduction exceeds bone conduction in both ears on the Rinne test. Step 1: Weber lateralizing away from the affected ear with a normal Rinne means sensorineural loss on the left, not conductive loss. Step 2: unilateral sensorineural loss with tinnitus points behind the cochlea to CN VIII. Step 3: the left corneal reflex is reduced, so the mass has grown far enough to stretch CN V, while facial movement is normal because CN VII motor fibers resist stretch. Step 4: an enhancing mass widening the internal acoustic canal fits vestibular schwannoma; a dural tail without canal widening would favor meningioma.

Neurofibromatosis type 1 (NF1) is one of the most common autosomal dominant disorders, affecting about 1 in 3,000 people. About half of cases are new mutations. Penetrance is essentially complete, but expressivity varies widely, even within one family. The NF1 gene on chromosome 17 encodes neurofibromin, a Ras GTPase-activating protein that speeds the hydrolysis of active Ras-GTP to inactive Ras-GDP. When a cell carrying the inherited mutation loses its second NF1 allele, Ras stays active and drives growth through the MAPK and PI3K pathways.

Most features involve tissues derived from the neural crest. Melanocyte changes produce cafe-au-lait macules (usually the first sign, in early childhood), freckling in the axillae and groin, and Lisch nodules, pigmented hamartomas of the iris that do not affect vision. Schwann cell proliferation produces neurofibromas.

A neurofibroma differs from a schwannoma in a way that explains its behavior. It is a mixture of Schwann cells, fibroblasts, perineurial-like cells, and mast cells, with the nerve's axons running through the tumor, so it cannot be separated from the nerve. Cutaneous neurofibromas are soft nodules that appear around puberty and increase with age. Plexiform neurofibromas are usually congenital, grow along long segments of a nerve trunk or plexus, and feel like a bag of worms under the skin. They can transform into a malignant peripheral nerve sheath tumor (MPNST), a high-grade sarcoma that NF1 patients develop at a lifetime risk of roughly 10%; new pain or rapid growth of a plexiform tumor suggests this change.

Other tumors follow from the same Ras activation. Optic pathway glioma, a pilocytic astrocytoma of the optic nerve or chiasm in young children, causes visual loss or proptosis, and hypothalamic involvement can cause precocious puberty. Pheochromocytoma, a tumor of adrenal chromaffin cells, occurs in a small percentage of patients and causes episodic or sustained hypertension from catecholamine release. Skeletal dysplasia (sphenoid wing, tibial pseudarthrosis, scoliosis) and learning disabilities are also common.

blocks.title: NF1 compared with NF2
rows: Merlin, cytoskeletal linker for contact inhibition
Few skin findings; posterior subcapsular cataract
blocks.caption: Both are tumor suppressor disorders with a second hit in each tumor; the lost protein and the cells it controls explain the different tumors.

blocks.predict: Why does a child with NF1 develop tumors in only some Schwann cells, even though every cell carries the mutation?
blocks.explain: One working NF1 allele still makes enough neurofibromin to control Ras; a tumor forms only in a cell that loses the second allele by a somatic event.
blocks.check: Reread the first paragraph of this section on loss of the second NF1 allele.

sections.title: Brain metastases and primary CNS lymphoma

blocks.text: Metastases are the most common intracranial tumors in adults. The brain receives about 15% of cardiac output, so tumor cells that reach the arterial circulation, usually after passing through or arising in the lung, are delivered there in large numbers. Lung cancer is the most frequent source, followed by breast cancer and melanoma; kidney and colorectal cancers are less common sources. Melanoma has the highest tendency to reach the brain relative to its frequency.

Tumor emboli lodge where arterioles narrow abruptly at the junction of gray and white matter and in the arterial border zones. Deposits are distributed roughly by blood flow, so most are in the cerebral hemispheres, fewer in the cerebellum, and few in the brainstem. They are often multiple, round, and sharply bordered, because they push brain aside rather than infiltrate it. New tumor vessels lack a blood-brain barrier, so even small metastases enhance and cause vasogenic edema out of proportion to their size. Melanoma, renal cell carcinoma, choriocarcinoma, and thyroid carcinoma metastases tend to bleed. Histology resembles the primary tumor and lacks GFAP. Leptomeningeal spread causes headache and multiple cranial nerve palsies.

Primary CNS lymphoma is a non-Hodgkin lymphoma confined to the brain, leptomeninges, spinal cord, or eyes, and almost all cases are diffuse large B cell lymphoma (CD20 positive). In immunocompetent patients it occurs mainly in older adults as a solitary, uniformly enhancing mass in the deep periventricular white matter, basal ganglia, or corpus callosum. The tumor cells cluster around blood vessels in concentric cuffs. Glucocorticoids trigger apoptosis of lymphoma cells, so a lesion can shrink after steroid exposure and a later biopsy may be nondiagnostic.

In AIDS with CD4 counts below about 50 cells per microliter, the tumor is almost always driven by Epstein-Barr virus. EBV latent proteins push infected B cells to proliferate and resist apoptosis, and without T cell surveillance they expand unchecked. These lesions are more often multiple, necrotic, and ring-enhancing, so they resemble cerebral toxoplasmosis.

blocks.title: Ring-enhancing lesions in advanced HIV
rows: EBV DNA in CSF by PCR
blocks.caption: These are tendencies rather than rules; tissue diagnosis is definitive.

blocks.title: A ring-enhancing lesion in AIDS
blocks.text: A 38-year-old with untreated HIV (CD4 count 30 cells per microliter) has confusion and right arm weakness. MRI shows one ring-enhancing lesion beside the left lateral ventricle extending into the corpus callosum. Step 1: at this CD4 count the two leading causes are toxoplasmosis and primary CNS lymphoma. Step 2: a single periventricular lesion involving the corpus callosum favors lymphoma; toxoplasmosis usually gives multiple basal ganglia and gray-white junction lesions. Step 3: EBV DNA in the CSF supports lymphoma because nearly all AIDS-related cases are EBV driven. Step 4: the tissue would show large atypical B cells cuffing vessels, CD20 positive, a diffuse large B cell lymphoma.

Retinoblastoma is the most common primary intraocular malignancy of childhood. It arises from primitive retinal cells and is usually diagnosed before age 5, at a younger age when bilateral. The RB1 gene on chromosome 13q14 encodes the retinoblastoma protein (pRb). In its unphosphorylated form pRb binds the transcription factor E2F and blocks entry from G1 into S phase; cyclin D with CDK4 or CDK6 phosphorylates pRb to release E2F when the cell should divide.

Retinoblastoma was the basis of the Knudson two-hit hypothesis. In hereditary cases, about 40% of the total, every cell carries a germline RB1 mutation, so only one somatic hit is needed in any retinal cell. Tumors are therefore earlier, bilateral, and multifocal. Most germline mutations are new, so many children have no family history, but each child of a hereditary survivor has about a 50% chance of inheriting it. In sporadic cases both hits must occur in the same retinal cell, so the tumor is unilateral, single, and later. Survivors of hereditary disease remain at risk for second cancers, most characteristically osteosarcoma, along with other sarcomas, particularly within a radiation field.

steps: Hereditary: germline RB1 mutation in every cell
One somatic hit in any retinal cell
Bilateral, multifocal, early tumors and later sarcomas
Sporadic: both RB1 copies normal at birth
Two somatic hits needed in one retinal cell
blocks.caption: The inherited first hit explains why the disease behaves as autosomal dominant in families while each tumor cell has lost both copies.

blocks.text: The classic sign is leukocoria: the white tumor reflects light where the normal red fundus reflex should be. Strabismus is the second most common sign, because a blind eye loses its fixation. The tumor often calcifies, and histology shows small round blue cells with Flexner-Wintersteiner rosettes (rings around a true central lumen, reflecting photoreceptor differentiation) and Homer Wright rosettes. It can spread along the optic nerve to the brain.

Uveal melanoma arises from melanocytes of the uveal tract, most often the choroid, and is the most common primary intraocular malignancy in adults (metastases to the eye are more common overall). Risk is higher in people with light skin and light irises. Unlike cutaneous melanoma it is not driven by ultraviolet damage or BRAF; it usually carries activating GNAQ or GNA11 mutations, and loss of BAP1 with monosomy 3 predicts metastasis. It causes blurred vision, flashes, floaters, or a field defect from retinal detachment, or is found on routine examination. The interior of the eye has no lymphatic drainage, so uveal melanoma spreads through the blood, most often to the liver, sometimes years after the eye tumor is found.

blocks.predict: A child has one tumor in one eye at age 3 and no family history. Can you be sure the mutation is not hereditary?
blocks.explain: No. Most germline RB1 mutations are new, so a hereditary case often has no family history; a single unilateral tumor only makes it less likely.
blocks.check: Compare with the two-hit flow and the paragraph on hereditary cases.

sections.title: Tuberous sclerosis and von Hippel-Lindau disease

blocks.text: Tuberous sclerosis complex is autosomal dominant, and about two thirds of cases are new mutations. It is caused by mutation of TSC1 (hamartin, chromosome 9) or TSC2 (tuberin, chromosome 16). Hamartin and tuberin form a complex that inactivates the small GTPase Rheb, which keeps mTORC1 switched off until growth signals arrive. Without the complex, mTORC1 stays active, driving protein synthesis and cell growth, so hamartomas form in many organs.

In the brain, cortical tubers are firm hamartomas of disorganized dysmorphic neurons, large balloon cells, and gliosis. They are highly epileptogenic, which explains infantile spasms, later focal epilepsy, intellectual disability, and autism. Subependymal nodules form along the walls of the lateral ventricles and often calcify. A subependymal giant cell astrocytoma (CNS WHO grade 1) grows from a nodule near the foramen of Monro and can block it, causing obstructive hydrocephalus. Skin findings include hypopigmented ash-leaf macules (accentuated under Wood lamp), facial angiofibromas, and shagreen patches. Cardiac rhabdomyomas are often detected before birth and usually regress afterward, and renal angiomyolipomas can bleed.

Von Hippel-Lindau disease is an autosomal dominant syndrome caused by mutation of VHL on chromosome 3p. The VHL protein is part of an E3 ubiquitin ligase. In normal oxygen, HIF-alpha is hydroxylated, VHL binds it, and the proteasome destroys it. Without VHL, HIF accumulates even when oxygen is normal, and cells act as if they were hypoxic, secreting VEGF, PDGF, and erythropoietin and increasing glucose uptake.

blocks.title: VHL loss and pseudohypoxia
steps: Second VHL allele lost in a susceptible cell
VEGF, PDGF, and erythropoietin genes switched on
Highly vascular tumors and sometimes polycythemia
blocks.caption: Constant HIF signaling explains why VHL tumors are richly vascular and why hemangioblastomas can raise the hematocrit.

blocks.text: The CNS lesion is the hemangioblastoma, a CNS WHO grade 1 tumor of lipid-laden stromal cells within a dense capillary network. It occurs in the cerebellum, brainstem, spinal cord, and retina. Cerebellar tumors are often a cyst with a mural nodule, causing ataxia and hydrocephalus, and some secrete erythropoietin. Retinal hemangioblastomas leak and cause retinal detachment and visual loss. Clear cell renal cell carcinoma, often multiple and bilateral, is a leading cause of death; pheochromocytoma and pancreatic cysts and neuroendocrine tumors also occur.

blocks.title: Tuberous sclerosis compared with von Hippel-Lindau disease
rows: Loss of Rheb control, mTORC1 overactive
Cortical tubers, subependymal nodules, giant cell astrocytoma
Clear cell renal carcinoma, pheochromocytoma, pancreatic lesions
blocks.caption: Both are autosomal dominant tumor suppressor syndromes; the pathway each gene controls predicts the lesions.

integration.text: Nervous system tumors are best approached by asking three questions. Anatomy answers where the mass is and therefore what it compresses or irritates: posterior fossa masses block the fourth ventricle, intraventricular masses block the foramina of Monro, cortical tumors cause seizures, and cerebellopontine angle masses affect CN VIII, then V, then VII. Histology identifies the cell lineage through rosettes, Rosenthal fibers, Verocay bodies, whorls, and pseudopalisading necrosis, supported by stains such as GFAP, synaptophysin, S-100, and epithelial membrane antigen. Molecular pathology now defines the main gliomas, so IDH status and 1p/19q codeletion carry as much weight as appearance.

Biochemistry and genetics explain why tumors form. Loss of neurofibromin leaves Ras active, loss of pRb removes the G1 checkpoint, loss of VHL creates pseudohypoxia, loss of TSC1 or TSC2 activates mTORC1, and mutant IDH produces an oncometabolite. Immunology links primary CNS lymphoma to loss of T cell surveillance of EBV and links opsoclonus-myoclonus to antitumor immunity that cross-reacts with neurons. A limit to remember is that age and site are probabilities, not rules: adults can have medulloblastoma and children can have glioblastoma, so the histologic and molecular findings decide the diagnosis when they are given.

summary: Children have mostly posterior fossa tumors (medulloblastoma, pilocytic astrocytoma, ependymoma); adults have mostly supratentorial tumors, and metastases are the most common intracranial tumors in adults.
Medulloblastoma is a grade 4 embryonal small round blue cell tumor of the vermis that causes obstructive hydrocephalus, truncal ataxia, and drop metastases through the CSF.
Meningioma is an extra-axial, dura-based tumor of arachnoid cap cells with whorls and psammoma bodies, linked to NF2 loss and prior radiation, and its symptoms depend on what it compresses.
Neuroblastoma is a neural crest tumor of young children that crosses the midline, raises urinary HVA and VMA, can cause opsoclonus-myoclonus, and behaves aggressively with MYCN amplification.

Glioblastoma is an IDH-wildtype grade 4 astrocytic tumor of older adults; hypoxia drives pseudopalisading necrosis, VEGF-driven microvascular proliferation, ring enhancement, and recurrence after resection.
Pilocytic astrocytoma is circumscribed, BRAF-altered, and curable; IDH-mutant astrocytoma and oligodendroglioma (1p/19q codeleted) are diffuse, seizure-producing tumors that cannot be fully removed.
Ganglioglioma causes chronic temporal lobe epilepsy, and central neurocytoma causes hydrocephalus by blocking the foramen of Monro.
Schwannomas push the nerve aside (Antoni A and B, Verocay bodies, S-100); vestibular schwannoma causes unilateral sensorineural hearing loss and tinnitus, and bilateral tumors define NF2.

NF1 (neurofibromin, a Ras GAP) causes cafe-au-lait macules, Lisch nodules, neurofibromas with MPNST risk, optic glioma, and pheochromocytoma; RB1, TSC1 or TSC2, and VHL losses explain retinoblastoma, tuberous sclerosis, and hemangioblastoma with renal carcinoma.
Primary CNS lymphoma is a diffuse large B cell lymphoma, EBV driven in AIDS, that must be separated from toxoplasmosis; uveal melanoma spreads by blood to the liver because the eye lacks lymphatics.

verify: Tumor names and grades follow the 2021 WHO Classification of CNS Tumors (CNS WHO grades in Arabic numerals, glioblastoma defined as IDH-wildtype). Confirm whether NABNE items still use older terms such as grade IV, secondary glioblastoma, or acoustic neuroma.
NF2 was renamed NF2-related schwannomatosis in 2022 consensus nomenclature; confirm which name NABNE uses.

Percentages are approximate and vary among sources: hereditary fraction of retinoblastoma (about 40%), MYCN amplification in neuroblastoma (about 20 to 25%), elevated HVA or VMA (about 90%), lifetime MPNST risk in NF1 (about 8 to 13%), and frequency of pheochromocytoma in NF1 (low single-digit percent).
Glioblastoma median survival is quoted as about 12 to 18 months depending on source and era; this chapter uses about 15 months.
The female to male ratio for intracranial meningioma is given as about 2:1 here; some sources quote up to 3:1.
NF1 diagnostic criteria were revised in 2021 (adding pathogenic NF1 variant and choroidal abnormalities); confirm which version NABNE expects if criteria are tested.

Requested new diagram names for a future revision: posterior-fossa-sagittal (vermis, fourth ventricle, cerebral aqueduct, and CSF outflow) and cpa-cranial-nerves (internal acoustic canal with CN VII and VIII and nearby CN V).
